rows.stem: The figure shows the voltage (V) versus the current (I) graphs for a wire at two temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\). One can conclude that :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem names neither line's slope, so the whole question lives in the drawing. What is drawn: a first-quadrant graph whose VERTICAL axis is labelled I and whose HORIZONTAL axis is labelled V, origin marked O, with two straight lines drawn from the origin, the upper labelled \(T_1\) and the lower labelled \(T_2\). WITHHELD: which of the two lines is the steeper, which is exactly what the four options discriminate. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
Read the axes before reading the lines. Here I is plotted VERTICALLY and V horizontally, so the slope of each line is
\(\text{slope} = \dfrac{I}{V} = \dfrac{1}{R}\)
and a STEEPER line means a SMALLER resistance, not a larger one.
From the figure the line labelled \(T_{1}\) is the steeper of the two, so
\(R_{1} < R_{2}\)
For a metallic wire the resistance RISES with temperature, because the lattice ions vibrate more vigorously, the electrons are scattered more often, the relaxation time \(\tau\) falls, and
\(R = \dfrac{m\,l}{n e^{2}\tau A}\)
grows as \(\tau\) shrinks. A smaller resistance therefore belongs to the LOWER temperature:
\(R_{1} < R_{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_{1} < T_{2}\)
One can conclude that \(T_{1} < T_{2}\).
The two options giving a numerical ratio, \(T_{2} = 2T_{1}\) and \(T_{1} = T_{2}/3\), cannot be right whatever the graph looks like: resistance is not proportional to temperature, and the relation between them depends on a temperature coefficient the question never supplies. A graph like this fixes an ORDER, never a ratio.

rows.stem: If \(R_s\) and \(R_p\) are the equivalent resistances of n resistors, each of value R, in series and parallel combinations respectively, then the value of \((R_s - R_p)\) is :
rows.solution:
Take the two combinations in turn, for n resistors each of value R.
IN SERIES the resistances simply add:
\(R_{s} = \underbrace{R + R + \cdots + R}_{n\ \text{terms}} = nR\)
IN PARALLEL the reciprocals add:
\(\dfrac{1}{R_{p}} = \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{R} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{R}}_{n\ \text{terms}} = \dfrac{n}{R} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R_{p} = \dfrac{R}{n}\)
Subtracting, over the common denominator n:
\(R_{s} - R_{p} = nR - \dfrac{R}{n} = \dfrac{n^{2}R - R}{n} = \left(\dfrac{n^{2} - 1}{n}\right)R\)
Two checks worth making. For \(n = 1\) there is only one resistor, series and parallel mean the same thing, and the expression correctly gives 0. And since \(R_{s}R_{p} = nR \times \dfrac{R}{n} = R^{2}\), the two combinations always have the same geometric mean — which is why the ratio \(\dfrac{R_{s}}{R_{p}} = n^{2}\) is the other standard result from this pair.

rows.subtopic: Biot-Savart Law and Field of a Circular Loop
rows.stem: The value of magnetic field at point O in the given figure is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem gives no geometry at all beyond the point O, so the drawing is the question. What is drawn: a current-carrying wire entering horizontally from the left with an arrow labelled I, rising into a curved section, and leaving horizontally to the right with an arrow labelled I; the two straight portions are collinear. The point O is marked on that line below the curve and a dashed line from O to the curve is labelled R. WITHHELD: the angle the curved section subtends at O, which is what the four options discriminate. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The wire has three parts, and the two straight ones contribute NOTHING at O.
For a current element the Biot-Savart law gives
\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,|d\vec{l} \times \hat{r}|}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^{2}}\)
From the figure the two straight leads are COLLINEAR with O: they lie along the very line on which O sits. So for every element of them \(d\vec{l}\) is either directly towards or directly away from O, making \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\) or \(180^{\circ}\) and \(\sin\theta = 0\). Each straight portion contributes exactly zero, however long it is.
That leaves the SEMICIRCULAR arc. Every element of it is at the same distance R from O and perpendicular to the line joining it to O, so the contributions add without any cancellation. A full circular loop would give \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2R}\), and a semicircle is half of that turn:
\(B = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2R} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{4R}\)
The field at O is \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{4R}\).
The options carrying \(\pi\) are the straight-wire formula \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi R}\) in disguise, which is what a reader gets by assuming the leads do the work. Here the geometry is arranged so that they cannot.

rows.stem: A piece of a diamagnetic material, free to move when placed in a uniform magnetic field :
rows.solution:
A piece of material in a magnetic field experiences a net FORCE only where the field is NON-UNIFORM. The two magnetic poles induced in the specimen are pulled in opposite directions, and if the field has the same strength everywhere those two pulls are equal and cancel exactly.
Written as a gradient, the force on a specimen of magnetic moment m is
\(F = m\dfrac{dB}{dx}\)
and the question states the field is UNIFORM, so \(\dfrac{dB}{dx} = 0\) and \(F = 0\) whatever the material.
So the piece does not move at all.
What diamagnetism decides is the DIRECTION a specimen would move if the field were non-uniform: a diamagnetic material is repelled from the stronger region towards the weaker, the opposite of a paramagnetic one. The word "uniform" in the stem removes that question entirely, and the three options describing motion are all there for a reader who answers the diamagnetism half without noticing the uniformity half.

rows.stem: A galvanometer can be converted into an ammeter of desired range by connecting a :
rows.solution:
A galvanometer is a sensitive instrument: it gives full-scale deflection for a very small current \(I_{g}\), often a few milliamperes. To read a much larger current I it must be protected, and the way to do that is to give most of the current somewhere else to go.
So a SMALL resistance, the shunt S, is connected in PARALLEL with the galvanometer. The two then share the current in inverse proportion to their resistances, and choosing S small sends the bulk of it through the shunt:
\(I_{g}G = (I - I_{g})S \quad\Longrightarrow\quad S = \dfrac{I_{g}G}{I - I_{g}}\)
The desired range is selected by choosing S. A galvanometer can therefore be converted into an ammeter by connecting a small resistance in parallel.
There is a second reason it must be in parallel, and it matters as much as the first. An ammeter is inserted INTO the circuit whose current it measures, so it must disturb that circuit as little as possible — its resistance should be nearly zero. A small shunt in parallel pulls the combined resistance DOWN; a series resistance would push it up, which is what converts a galvanometer into a VOLTMETER instead.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: A proton and an \(\alpha\)-particle enter with the same velocity \(\vec{v}\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) such that \(\vec{v} \perp \vec{B}\). The ratio of the radii of their paths is :
rows.solution:
In a magnetic field a charged particle of momentum mv moves on a circle of radius
\(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\)
Both particles enter with the SAME velocity v into the SAME field B, so those cancel in the ratio and
\(r \propto \dfrac{m}{q}\)
For the proton, mass m and charge e. For the \(\alpha\)-particle, a helium nucleus of two protons and two neutrons, mass 4m and charge 2e. Hence
\(\dfrac{r_{p}}{r_{\alpha}} = \dfrac{m/e}{4m/2e} = \dfrac{m}{e} \times \dfrac{2e}{4m} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
The ratio of the radii is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Note that the \(\alpha\)-particle takes the WIDER circle even though it carries twice the charge: its mass is four times greater, and mass is in the numerator. The answer 2 is what comes out if the ratio is written the other way up, and the question fixes the order by naming the proton first.

rows.subtopic: Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
rows.stem: A vertically held bar magnet is dropped along the axis of a copper ring having a cut as shown in the diagram. The acceleration of the falling magnet is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — the stem already states in words that the ring is a copper ring HAVING A CUT, which is the whole discriminator, so the row is answerable from text alone. What is drawn: a rectangular bar magnet with S at its upper end and N at its lower end, a downward arrow beside it, and below it a horizontal circular ring drawn in perspective with a clearly visible gap in its near side. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The ring is CUT, and that single word settles the question.
Ordinarily a magnet falling towards a closed conducting ring changes the flux through it, an emf is induced, a current flows, and by Lenz's law that current opposes the approach — the ring pushes back, and the magnet falls with an acceleration LESS than g.
A cut ring is not a closed circuit. An emf is still induced in it, since the flux through it still changes, but there is no complete conducting path, so NO INDUCED CURRENT can flow. With no current there is no magnetic moment, no opposing force, and nothing acting on the magnet but gravity.
The acceleration of the falling magnet is therefore g.
This is the cleanest demonstration that Lenz's law costs energy: the retardation in the closed-ring case is paid for by the heat \(I^{2}R\) dissipated in the ring, and where no current flows there is nothing to pay for and nothing to retard. The same magnet dropped through an intact copper ring, or a copper pipe, falls noticeably slowly.

rows.stem: An ac source is connected to a resistor and an inductor in series. The voltage across the resistor and inductor are 8 V and 6 V respectively. The voltage of the source is :
rows.solution:
The voltages across a resistor and an inductor do NOT add arithmetically, because they are not in phase. Across a resistor the voltage is in phase with the current; across an inductor it LEADS the current by \(90^{\circ}\).
So the two are perpendicular in the phasor diagram and combine like the two sides of a right angle:
\(V = \sqrt{V_{R}^{2} + V_{L}^{2}}\)
\(V = \sqrt{(8)^{2} + (6)^{2}} = \sqrt{64 + 36} = \sqrt{100}\)
\(V = 10\ \mathrm{V}\)
The source voltage is 10 V.
The number to notice is that 10 V is LESS than the arithmetic sum 14 V, which is one of the options and is the answer a reader gets by adding. It is the characteristic signature of an ac circuit: the individual voltmeter readings can total more than the supply reading without anything being wrong, because the two maxima never occur at the same instant.

rows.stem: Two coherent waves, each of intensity \(I_0\), produce interference pattern on a screen. The average intensity of light on the screen is :
rows.solution:
At a point where two coherent waves meet with phase difference \(\phi\), the resultant intensity is
\(I = I_{1} + I_{2} + 2\sqrt{I_{1}I_{2}}\cos\phi\)
With \(I_{1} = I_{2} = I_{0}\) this becomes \(I = 2I_{0}(1 + \cos\phi) = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}\), which runs from \(4I_{0}\) at the bright fringes down to 0 at the dark ones.
The question asks for the AVERAGE over the whole screen. Averaging the expression above, the first two terms are constants and survive, while the interference term contains \(\cos\phi\), whose average over a full range of phase is ZERO:
\(\langle I \rangle = I_{0} + I_{0} + 0 = 2I_{0}\)
The average intensity on the screen is \(2I_{0}\).
That it must come out this way follows from energy conservation alone, without any algebra: interference does not create or destroy light, it only REDISTRIBUTES it. The energy removed from the dark fringes is exactly what makes the bright fringes four times \(I_{0}\) rather than two, so the average is bound to be the plain sum of the two beams.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: The work function of a material is \(2{\cdot}21\) eV. Which of the following **cannot** produce photoelectrons from it ?
rows.solution:
Photoemission needs a photon whose energy exceeds the work function, and photon energy rises as wavelength falls:
\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1240}{\lambda(\mathrm{nm})}\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Among the four colours offered, RED has the longest wavelength and therefore the SMALLEST photon energy. Taking red at about 700 nm:
\(E_{red} = \dfrac{1240}{700} \approx 1{\cdot}77\ \mathrm{eV}\)
which is less than the work function \(2{\cdot}21\) eV, so red light cannot eject an electron.
The others all clear the bar. Green at about 550 nm gives \(2{\cdot}25\) eV, blue at about 470 nm gives \(2{\cdot}64\) eV, violet at about 420 nm gives \(2{\cdot}95\) eV.
So red light cannot produce photoelectrons.
Making the red beam brighter will not help, and that is the point Einstein's explanation turns on: intensity sets how MANY photons arrive, never how much energy each one carries. A single photon must do the whole job by itself, so a beam below the threshold frequency ejects nothing no matter how intense it is. Green is the near miss here, clearing \(2{\cdot}21\) eV by only a little.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: The momentum (in kg m/s) of a photon of frequency \(6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{14}\) Hz is :
rows.solution:
A photon has no rest mass, but it does carry momentum, given by
\(p = \dfrac{E}{c} = \dfrac{h\nu}{c}\)
Substituting \(h = 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\), \(\nu = 6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}\) and \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\):
\(p = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{14}}{3 \times 10^{8}}\)
The numerator is \(39{\cdot}78 \times 10^{-20} = 3{\cdot}978 \times 10^{-19}\), so
\(p = \dfrac{3{\cdot}978 \times 10^{-19}}{3 \times 10^{8}}\)
\(p = 1{\cdot}326 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\)
The momentum is \(1{\cdot}326 \times 10^{-27}\) kg m/s.
The distractor \(3{\cdot}978 \times 10^{-19}\) is the photon's ENERGY in joules, offered as if it were a momentum, and \(6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-25}\) is what appears if the frequency is used where the wavelength belongs. Dividing by c is the whole step that converts one into the other.

rows.stem: Inside a nucleus, the nuclear forces between proton and proton, proton and neutron, neutron and neutron are \(F_{pp}\), \(F_{pn}\) and \(F_{nn}\) respectively. Then :
rows.solution:
The nuclear force is CHARGE-INDEPENDENT. Between any two nucleons at the same separation it is the same strength, whether the pair is proton-proton, proton-neutron or neutron-neutron:
\(F_{pp} = F_{pn} = F_{nn}\)
That is a property of the nuclear force itself, and it is one of the main pieces of evidence that protons and neutrons are two states of a single particle as far as the strong interaction is concerned.
A caution about what the statement does NOT say. Two protons ALSO repel each other electrostatically, so the NET force between them differs from that between two neutrons. But the electrostatic force is a separate interaction, and the question asks about the nuclear forces, which are equal.
Supporting evidence comes from the mirror nuclei: \(^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\) and \(^{3}_{2}\mathrm{He}\) have their proton and neutron numbers interchanged, and their binding energies agree once the Coulomb repulsion is subtracted — exactly what charge-independence predicts.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : In a reflecting telescope, the image does not have chromatic aberration.
Reason (R) : Chromatic aberration occurs only due to refraction of light through an optical medium.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are TRUE, and the reason is the correct explanation.
CHROMATIC ABERRATION arises because the refractive index of a medium varies with wavelength. A lens therefore has a slightly different focal length for each colour,
\(\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}}\right]\)
with n larger for violet than for red, so violet focuses nearer the lens and the image is fringed with colour. Every term in that defect comes from refraction.
A REFLECTING TELESCOPE uses a concave MIRROR as its objective, and reflection is governed by
\(i = r\)
which contains no refractive index at all. The law of reflection is the same for every wavelength, so all colours are brought to exactly the same focus and no chromatic aberration is produced.
Both the assertion and the reason are true and the reason explains the assertion. This is the main reason every large modern telescope is a reflector: a mirror is free of chromatic aberration by construction, can be supported across its whole back rather than only at its rim, and needs only one surface figured instead of two.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : A hole is an apparent free particle with effective positive electronic charge.
Reason (R) : A hole is not necessarily a vacancy left behind by an electron in the valence band.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
The ASSERTION is TRUE. A hole behaves in every measurable way like a free particle carrying a charge \(+e\): it drifts along the applied field, it has its own mobility, it contributes to the current, and it is deflected by a magnetic field as a positive carrier would be. That is what "apparent free particle with effective positive electronic charge" records — the hole is not a real particle, but the mathematics of a valence band with one electron missing is identical to that of a single positive particle moving freely.
The REASON is FALSE, because it denies exactly what a hole is. A hole IS the vacancy left in the valence band when an electron leaves it. When a neighbouring bound electron moves into that vacancy, the vacancy itself shifts the other way, and that migrating vacancy is what we call the hole's motion.
So the assertion is true but the reason is false.
It is worth keeping the two halves distinct: the hole is genuinely a vacancy, which is the reason's error, AND it is legitimately treated as a positive particle, which is the assertion's claim. The first is what it is; the second is how it behaves.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : X-rays are produced when slow moving electrons are stopped by a metal target of high atomic number.
Reason (R) : X-rays consist of low-energy photons.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are FALSE.
The ASSERTION is false because X-rays require FAST-moving electrons, not slow ones. Electrons are accelerated through a large potential difference, typically tens of kilovolts, and it is their kinetic energy that is converted into radiation when the target stops them:
\(eV = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{min}}\)
So the shortest wavelength produced is fixed by the accelerating voltage. Slow electrons carry too little energy to produce X-rays at all. (That the target has a high atomic number is correct and is why tungsten is used — a heavier nucleus decelerates the electrons more strongly and yields a higher output.)
The REASON is false in the opposite direction. X-ray photons are HIGH-energy, not low. With wavelengths from about 1 nm down to \(10^{-3}\) nm, their energies run from roughly 1 keV to over 100 keV, thousands of times the few eV of a visible photon. That energy is precisely why X-rays penetrate flesh and are used to image bone.
Both the assertion and the reason are false, and the two errors are connected: it is the high photon energy of the reason that requires the fast electrons of the assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The binding energy per nucleon is practically constant for mass number in the range \((30 < A < 170)\).
Reason (R) : Nuclear forces between the nucleons for mass numbers in the range \((30 < A < 170)\) are not short-range.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
The ASSERTION is TRUE. Over the range \(30 < A < 170\) the binding energy per nucleon is very nearly constant at about 8.5 MeV, the flat plateau of the binding-energy curve, peaking near \(^{56}\mathrm{Fe}\).
The REASON is FALSE, and it states the opposite of the truth. Nuclear forces ARE short-range, acting only over about 2 to 3 fm, roughly the size of a couple of nucleons.
That short range is in fact the CAUSE of the constancy the assertion describes, which is what makes the reason's error so costly. Because the force reaches only as far as its immediate neighbours, a nucleon deep inside a nucleus is bound by a FIXED number of partners, no matter how large the nucleus grows. This is the SATURATION of nuclear forces. Adding more nucleons adds more of the same local binding without increasing any one nucleon's share, so
\(\dfrac{E_{b}}{A} \approx \text{constant} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E_{b} \propto A\)
Had the force been long-range like gravity or electrostatics, every nucleon would interact with all \((A-1)\) others, the total binding would grow as \(A^{2}\), and \(\dfrac{E_{b}}{A}\) would climb steadily with A instead of flattening.
So the assertion is true but the reason is false.

rows.stem: Find the equivalent resistance between points A and B for the network shown in the figure.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem names no resistance value and no connectivity, so the entire question is in the drawing. What can safely be said: terminal A on the left is joined through a \(1\ \Omega\) resistor to the left-hand node of a diamond-shaped network whose right-hand node is terminal B. The remaining eight resistors carry the values \(5\ \Omega\), \(5\ \Omega\), \(10\ \Omega\), \(25\ \Omega\), \(20\ \Omega\), \(15\ \Omega\), \(10\ \Omega\) and \(30\ \Omega\). WITHHELD: which resistor sits on which branch and how the branches join, because that connectivity IS the question. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
Read the drawing carefully before computing anything: the vertical branch HOPS OVER the horizontal one in the middle of the network. That little arc is the standard notation for two wires that CROSS WITHOUT CONNECTING, and everything here turns on it.
So the network between C and B is three separate paths from C to B, plus one bridge:
TOP PATH: \(5\ \Omega\) then \(10\ \Omega\) in series \(= 15\ \Omega\)
MIDDLE PATH: \(25\ \Omega\) then \(20\ \Omega\) in series \(= 45\ \Omega\)
BOTTOM PATH: \(15\ \Omega\) then \(30\ \Omega\) in series \(= 45\ \Omega\)
BRIDGE: the \(5\ \Omega\) and \(10\ \Omega\) of the vertical branch, joining the TOP node to the BOTTOM node, crossing the middle path without touching it.
Now test the bridge. It connects the junction of the top path to the junction of the bottom path, so it sits across a Wheatstone arrangement whose arms are \(5, 10\) on one side and \(15, 30\) on the other:
\(\dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2} \qquad \dfrac{15}{30} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
The ratios are EQUAL, so the bridge is BALANCED. Its two ends are at the same potential, no current flows through it, and it can be ignored entirely.
That leaves three simple parallel paths between C and B:
\(\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{45} + \dfrac{1}{45} = \dfrac{3 + 1 + 1}{45} = \dfrac{5}{45} = \dfrac{1}{9}\)
\(R = 9\ \Omega\)
Finally the \(1\ \Omega\) between A and C is in series with all of this:
\(R_{AB} = 1 + 9\)
\(R_{AB} = 10\ \Omega\)
The equivalent resistance between A and B is \(10\ \Omega\). Had the vertical branch been CONNECTED to the horizontal one at the crossing, the three paths would not be independent, the balance argument would not apply, and the answer would not be a round number at all — which is a fair sign that reading the hop correctly is the intended first step.

rows.stem: Find the intensity at a point on the screen in Young's double slit experiment, at which the interfering waves of intensity \(I_0\) each, have a path difference of (i) \(\dfrac{\lambda}{3}\), and (ii) \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\).
rows.solution:
Convert each path difference into a phase difference, then use the two-source intensity formula.
The relation between them is
\(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \Delta x\)
and for two sources of equal intensity \(I_{0}\) the resultant is
\(I = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\Delta\phi}{2}\)
(i) PATH DIFFERENCE \(\dfrac{\lambda}{3}\):
\(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
\(I = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 4I_{0}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = 4I_{0} \times \dfrac{1}{4}\)
\(I = I_{0}\)
(ii) PATH DIFFERENCE \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\):
\(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = \pi\)
\(I = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 4I_{0} \times 0\)
\(I = 0\)
So the intensities are \(I_{0}\) and 0 respectively.
The second result is worth pausing on: a path difference of half a wavelength gives complete darkness even though each slit on its own delivers \(I_{0}\). The first is the more instructive of the two though — at one-third of a wavelength the intensity happens to equal what a SINGLE slit would give, so that particular point on the screen is indistinguishable in brightness from no interference at all.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A point source of light in air is kept at a distance of 12 cm in front of a convex spherical surface of glass of refractive index \(1{\cdot}5\) and radius of curvature 30 cm. Find the nature and position of the image formed.
rows.solution:
This is refraction at a SINGLE spherical surface, not a lens, so use
\(\dfrac{n_{2}}{v} - \dfrac{n_{1}}{u} = \dfrac{n_{2} - n_{1}}{R}\)
Fix the signs first, measuring everything from the surface with light travelling left to right. The object is real and 12 cm in front, so \(u = -12\) cm. The surface is convex towards the incoming light, so its centre of curvature lies on the outgoing side and \(R = +30\) cm. Light passes from air into glass, so \(n_{1} = 1\) and \(n_{2} = 1{\cdot}5\).
Substituting:
\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} - \dfrac{1}{(-12)} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5 - 1}{30}\)
\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{30} = \dfrac{1}{60}\)
\(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{v} = \dfrac{1}{60} - \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{1 - 5}{60} = -\dfrac{4}{60} = -\dfrac{1}{15}\)
\(v = -1{\cdot}5 \times 15\)
\(v = -22{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The NEGATIVE sign says the image lies on the SAME side as the object, which means no light actually converges there: the image is VIRTUAL and erect, formed 22.5 cm in front of the surface.
The object is too close for the surface to converge the light: \(\dfrac{1}{60}\) is smaller than \(\dfrac{1}{12}\), so the bracket cannot be made positive, and the refracted rays still diverge after crossing the surface. They merely diverge LESS steeply than before, which is what places the virtual image further away than the object.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: A laser beam of frequency \(3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{14}\) Hz produces average power of 9 mW. Find (i) the energy of photon of the beam, and (ii) the number of photons emitted per second on an average by the source.
rows.solution:
(i) ENERGY OF ONE PHOTON. From the Planck relation,
\(E = h\nu = 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{14}\)
\(E = 1{\cdot}99 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)
(about 1.24 eV, which puts this beam in the near infrared.)
(ii) NUMBER OF PHOTONS PER SECOND. The power is the energy delivered per second, and the beam delivers that energy in photons of the size just computed, so the number per second is simply the power divided by the energy of one:
\(N = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{-3}}{1{\cdot}99 \times 10^{-19}}\)
\(N = 4{\cdot}5 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{photons\ per\ second}\)
The scale of that number is the reason the granularity of light goes unnoticed in ordinary experience. A source of only 9 milliwatts — far dimmer than a household bulb — still emits forty-five thousand million million photons every second, so the arrival of individual photons blurs into a perfectly smooth, continuous beam. The quantum nature shows itself only in experiments like photoemission, where a single photon must act alone.

rows.stem: A right angled isosceles glass prism ABC is kept in contact with an equilateral triangular prism DBC as shown in the figure. Both prisms are made of the same glass of refractive index \(1{\cdot}6\). Trace the path of the ray MN incident normally on face AB as it passes through the combination.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem asks the candidate to TRACE a path through a specific geometry that only the drawing fixes. What is drawn: triangle ABC with A at the top, B below it and C to the right of B, so that AB is a vertical face and BC a horizontal face; the angle at A is marked 45°. A horizontal ray arrives from the left, its tail labelled M, and meets face AB at a point N marked with a right-angle symbol. Below BC an inverted triangle DBC is drawn sharing the face BC, with D at the bottom and the angles at B and C both marked 60°. WITHHELD: the traced path itself — where the ray reflects, refracts or emerges — which is the answer. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
Find the critical angle first, since every step depends on comparing an angle with it:
\(\sin i_{c} = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = \dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}6} = 0{\cdot}625 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad i_{c} \approx 38{\cdot}7^{\circ}\)
AT FACE AB. The ray MN is incident NORMALLY, so it enters without bending and travels straight on to the face AC.
AT FACE AC. Prism ABC is right-angled isosceles with the right angle at B, so AC makes \(45^{\circ}\) with the ray. Since
\(45^{\circ} > 38{\cdot}7^{\circ}\)
the ray is TOTALLY INTERNALLY REFLECTED. It turns through \(90^{\circ}\) and now travels vertically downwards.
AT FACE BC. This is the face the two prisms share. Both are made of the SAME glass and are in contact, so BC is not an optical interface at all — there is no change of medium and the ray crosses it undeviated, passing into the equilateral prism DBC.
AT FACE DC. The equilateral prism's faces make \(60^{\circ}\) with BC, so the vertically-travelling ray meets DC at \(60^{\circ}\) to its normal. Again
\(60^{\circ} > 38{\cdot}7^{\circ}\)
so the ray is TOTALLY INTERNALLY REFLECTED a second time, and now travels downwards and to the left.
AT FACE BD. Reflected off DC, the ray arrives at BD along its NORMAL, at \(0^{\circ}\) incidence. It therefore emerges without bending, travelling perpendicular to BD.
So the path is: straight in through AB, total internal reflection at AC, straight across BC, total internal reflection at DC, and out through BD undeviated — the ray having been turned through \(150^{\circ}\) in all.
Note that no refraction ever occurs inside the combination: at every face the ray either meets the surface normally or exceeds the critical angle. That is what makes the trace exact rather than approximate, and it is why a pair of prisms like this can steer a beam with no colour fringing at all.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: In an n-type semiconductor electron-hole combination is a continuous process at room temperature. Yet the electron concentration is always greater than the hole concentration in it. Explain.
rows.solution:
Count where each kind of carrier comes from, and the asymmetry is immediate.
THE ELECTRONS have TWO sources. Each pentavalent donor atom contributes one electron that needs almost no energy to break free, and in addition every thermally broken covalent bond contributes one. So
\(n_{e} = (\text{electrons from donors}) + (\text{electrons from broken bonds})\)
THE HOLES have only ONE source. A donor atom leaves behind no vacancy — its fifth electron was never in a bond — so donors create no holes at all. Every hole in the sample comes from a thermally broken bond:
\(n_{h} = (\text{holes from broken bonds})\)
Since the thermal contribution is the same for both, and the electrons have the whole donor contribution on top of it, \(n_{e}\) exceeds \(n_{h}\) at every moment. The doping concentration is typically millions of times the intrinsic one, so the excess is enormous, not marginal.
Electron-hole recombination is continuous, exactly as the question says, but it does not level the two out. Recombination consumes electrons and holes in EQUAL numbers, one of each, so it removes the same amount from both and cannot close a gap. At equilibrium generation balances recombination, and that balance fixes the PRODUCT rather than the difference:
\(n_{e}n_{h} = n_{i}^{2}\)
So the flood of donor electrons actually drives the hole concentration BELOW its intrinsic value, since the product must stay fixed while \(n_{e}\) rises. Recombination is the very mechanism that suppresses the holes.

rows.stem:
What is the difference between 'emf' and 'terminal voltage' of a cell ?
Two cells of emfs \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) and internal resistances \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are connected in parallel. Derive an expression for the emf and internal resistance of the equivalent cell.
rows.solution:
DIFFERENCE BETWEEN EMF AND TERMINAL VOLTAGE.
The EMF is the potential difference across the cell's terminals when NO current is drawn, that is on OPEN circuit. It is a property of the cell alone, fixed by its chemistry, and does not depend on the external circuit.
The TERMINAL VOLTAGE is the potential difference across the terminals when the cell is actually delivering current, that is on CLOSED circuit. Part of the emf is spent driving the current through the cell's own internal resistance, so
\(V = \varepsilon - Ir\)
and the terminal voltage DOES depend on the external resistance, falling further the more current is drawn. The emf is the cause, the terminal voltage the effect.
TWO CELLS IN PARALLEL. Let cells of emf \(E_{1}, E_{2}\) and internal resistances \(r_{1}, r_{2}\) be joined between the same two points, delivering branch currents \(I_{1}\) and \(I_{2}\). Because they are in parallel, both have the SAME terminal voltage V, and their currents add:
\(V = E_{1} - I_{1}r_{1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_{1} = \dfrac{E_{1} - V}{r_{1}}\)
\(V = E_{2} - I_{2}r_{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_{2} = \dfrac{E_{2} - V}{r_{2}}\)
\(I = I_{1} + I_{2} = \dfrac{E_{1} - V}{r_{1}} + \dfrac{E_{2} - V}{r_{2}}\)
Collecting the terms in V:
\(I = \left(\dfrac{E_{1}}{r_{1}} + \dfrac{E_{2}}{r_{2}}\right) - V\left(\dfrac{1}{r_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{r_{2}}\right)\)
\(I = \dfrac{E_{1}r_{2} + E_{2}r_{1}}{r_{1}r_{2}} - V\,\dfrac{r_{1} + r_{2}}{r_{1}r_{2}}\)
Comparing this with the single equivalent cell it must imitate, \(I = \dfrac{E_{eq} - V}{r_{eq}}\), and matching the two pieces:
\(E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_{1}r_{2} + E_{2}r_{1}}{r_{1} + r_{2}} \qquad\text{and}\qquad r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_{1}r_{2}}{r_{1} + r_{2}}\)
The equivalent internal resistance is just the two internal resistances in parallel, as expected. The equivalent emf is a WEIGHTED average in which each emf is weighted by the OTHER cell's internal resistance — so the cell with the smaller internal resistance has the greater say, which is why a fresh cell in parallel with a worn one is dragged down less than a plain average would suggest.

rows.stem:
A rectangular loop carries a current of 1 A. A straight long wire carrying 2 A current is kept near the loop in the same plane as shown in the figure.
Find :
(i) the torque acting on the loop, and
(ii) the magnitude and direction of the net force on the loop.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — every dimension in this question is printed on the drawing and none of it is in the stem. What is drawn: a long straight vertical wire on the left labelled 2 A; to its right a rectangle labelled 1 A whose width is marked 1 cm and whose height is marked 5 cm, with the horizontal gap between the wire and the nearer vertical side of the rectangle also marked 1 cm. WITHHELD: the arrow senses marked on the two currents, which are what decide the direction asked for in part (ii). Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
(i) TORQUE ON THE LOOP.
The torque on a current loop in a magnetic field is
\(\vec{\tau} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tau = mB\sin\theta\)
The loop's magnetic moment \(\vec{m}\) is perpendicular to its own plane. The field of the long straight wire, at every point of that plane, is also perpendicular to the plane, since the field of a straight wire circles it. So \(\vec{m}\) and \(\vec{B}\) are PARALLEL, \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\), and
\(\tau = mB\sin 0^{\circ}\)
\(\tau = 0\)
The torque is zero. The loop is not turned at all, only pulled.
(ii) NET FORCE ON THE LOOP.
Only the two arms PARALLEL to the wire feel a force along the line joining them to it; the two perpendicular arms carry equal and opposite forces that cancel. The two parallel arms sit at DIFFERENT distances, so their forces do not cancel — and that is the whole of this part.
The force per unit length between parallel currents is \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi r}\), attractive for parallel currents and repulsive for antiparallel ones. From the figure the wire carries \(I_{1} = 2\) A, the loop \(I_{2} = 1\) A, the arms are \(l = 5\ \mathrm{cm} = 5 \times 10^{-2}\) m long, and they lie at \(r_{1} = 1\ \mathrm{cm} = 10^{-2}\) m and \(r_{2} = 2\ \mathrm{cm} = 2 \times 10^{-2}\) m.
The NEAR arm carries current in the SAME direction as the wire, so it is ATTRACTED. The FAR arm, being the return side of the loop, carries it oppositely and is REPELLED. Since attraction acts at the smaller distance it wins, and the net force is their difference:
\(F_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}l}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{r_{2}}\right)\)
\(F_{net} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2 \times 1 \times 5 \times 10^{-2}}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{1}{10^{-2}} - \dfrac{1}{2 \times 10^{-2}}\right)\)
\(F_{net} = \left(2 \times 10^{-7} \times 2 \times 5 \times 10^{-2}\right) \times \left(100 - 50\right)\)
\(F_{net} = 2 \times 10^{-8} \times 50\)
\(F_{net} = 1 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{N}\)
The net force is \(1 \times 10^{-6}\) N, directed TOWARDS the long straight wire.
A loop near a straight wire is therefore pulled bodily towards it without being rotated — the field is non-uniform, which gives the net force, but it points the same way through the whole loop, which is why there is no torque.

rows.stem: State Lenz's law. A rod MN of length L is rotated about an axis passing through its end M perpendicular to its length, with a constant angular velocity \(\omega\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) parallel to the axis. Obtain an expression for emf induced between its ends.
rows.solution:
LENZ'S LAW. The polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which OPPOSES the change in magnetic flux that produced it.
It is a statement of energy conservation: if the induced effects aided the change instead of opposing it, the change would grow without limit and energy would be created from nothing.
EMF ACROSS THE ROTATING ROD. The rod MN of length L turns about the end M with angular velocity \(\omega\), in a field \(\vec{B}\) parallel to the axis and hence perpendicular to the plane the rod sweeps.
The difficulty is that different parts of the rod move at different speeds — a point at distance r from the axis has \(v = \omega r\) — so the emf cannot be written down for the rod as a whole. Take instead a small element of length dr at distance r. It moves at right angles to the field with speed \(\omega r\), so the emf across it is
\(d\varepsilon = B\,v\,dr = B(\omega r)dr\)
Every element lies along the same rod, so their emfs are in SERIES and simply add. Integrating from the axis at \(r = 0\) out to the far end at \(r = L\):
\(\varepsilon = \int_{0}^{L} B\omega r\,dr = B\omega\left[\dfrac{r^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{L}\)
\(\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{2}BL^{2}\omega\)
The same result follows from the flux directly. In time t the rod sweeps the sector MQN of angle \(\theta = \omega t\), whose area is \(\dfrac{1}{2}L^{2}\theta\), so
\(\phi = B \times \dfrac{1}{2}L^{2}\theta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \varepsilon = \dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2}BL^{2}\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2}BL^{2}\omega\)
Note the factor of \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) and the SQUARE on L. Treating the whole rod as though it moved at the speed of its far end would give \(BL^{2}\omega\), twice too much; the half is the average of the speed over the rod's length, and it is the commonest error in this derivation.

rows.stem: Define 'self-inductance' of a coil. Derive an expression for self-inductance of a long solenoid of cross-sectional area A and length \(l\), having n turns per unit length.
rows.solution:
SELF-INDUCTANCE of a coil is the ratio of the total flux linkage through the coil to the current flowing in it:
\(L = \dfrac{N\phi_{B}}{I}\)
Equivalently, it is the flux linked with the coil when unit current flows through it. It depends only on the coil's geometry and on the medium in its core, never on the current — a coil of given shape has a fixed L.
It can also be defined through the emf it opposes: since \(\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\), the self-inductance is the magnitude of the emf induced when the current changes at 1 A per second.
EXPRESSION FOR A LONG SOLENOID. Let the solenoid have length l, cross-sectional area A and n turns per unit length, so its total number of turns is \(N = nl\).
The field well inside a long solenoid is uniform and given by
\(B = \mu_{0}nI\)
Each turn encloses the area A, so the flux through one turn is \(\phi_{B} = BA = \mu_{0}nIA\). All N turns link this same flux, so the total flux linkage is
\(N\phi_{B} = (nl)(\mu_{0}nIA) = \mu_{0}n^{2}AlI\)
Dividing by the current, which cancels as it must:
\(L = \dfrac{N\phi_{B}}{I}\)
\(L = \mu_{0}n^{2}Al\)
Everything on the right is geometry, which is the point of the result. Two features are worth noting: L depends on the SQUARE of the turn density, because n enters once through the field and once through the number of turns linking it; and writing \(Al = V\), the solenoid's volume, gives \(L = \mu_{0}n^{2}V\). Filling the core with a material of relative permeability \(\mu_{r}\) multiplies L by that factor, which is why iron-cored coils have inductances thousands of times larger.

rows.stem: Name the electromagnetic wave used (i) in radar, (ii) in eye surgery and (iii) as diagnostic tool in medicine. Write their wavelength range also.
rows.solution:
(i) IN RADAR — MICROWAVES.
Wavelength range: about 0.1 m down to 1 mm.
They are produced by special vacuum tubes such as klystrons and magnetrons. Their short wavelength lets them be formed into a narrow beam, which is what makes direction-finding possible, and they reflect strongly off metal objects such as aircraft.
(ii) IN EYE SURGERY — ULTRAVIOLET.
Wavelength range: about 400 nm down to 1 nm.
Ultraviolet from an excimer laser can be focused to a very fine spot, allowing the precise reshaping of the cornea in LASIK surgery. (Infrared lasers, wavelength range about 1 mm down to 700 nm, are also used in ophthalmic procedures and are equally acceptable here.)
(iii) AS A DIAGNOSTIC TOOL IN MEDICINE — X-RAYS.
Wavelength range: about 1 nm down to \(10^{-3}\) nm.
X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, so a photographic plate behind the patient records a shadow image of the skeleton.
Reading the three together shows the wavelength falling by roughly six orders of magnitude from the first to the third, and it is that fall — and the rise in photon energy \(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\) which accompanies it — that decides what each is good for. Microwaves travel and reflect, ultraviolet cuts, and X-rays penetrate.

rows.stem: Draw a ray diagram showing the image formation when a concave mirror produces a real, inverted and magnified image of an object and hence obtain the mirror formula.
rows.solution:
RAY DIAGRAM. A concave mirror gives a real, inverted and MAGNIFIED image when the object lies BETWEEN the focus F and the centre of curvature C. Place the object AB on the principal axis with its foot B, and draw two standard rays from the top point A:
A ray PARALLEL to the principal axis, which after reflection passes through F.
A ray through F, which after reflection travels parallel to the axis.
The two reflected rays actually meet beyond C, at \(A'\), and dropping a perpendicular to the axis gives the image \(A'B'\) — real, inverted and larger than the object. Mark the pole P, the object distance u, the image distance v and the focal length f, with arrows on every ray.
DERIVING THE MIRROR FORMULA. Let the parallel ray strike the mirror at M, so that MP equals the object height AB.
In \(\triangle A'B'F\) and \(\triangle MPF\), both right-angled and sharing the vertical angle at F, the triangles are SIMILAR:
\(\dfrac{A'B'}{MP} = \dfrac{B'F}{FP} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{A'B'}{AB} = \dfrac{B'F}{FP} \qquad (\because MP = AB) \qquad \ldots(1)\)
In \(\triangle A'B'P\) and \(\triangle ABP\), similar because the incident and reflected rays at the pole make equal angles with the axis:
\(\dfrac{A'B'}{AB} = \dfrac{PB'}{PB} \qquad \ldots(2)\)
Both left-hand sides are the same, so the right-hand sides are equal:
\(\dfrac{B'F}{FP} = \dfrac{PB'}{PB}\)
Writing \(B'F = PB' - PF\):
\(\dfrac{PB' - PF}{FP} = \dfrac{PB'}{PB}\)
Now insert the sign convention. Distances are measured from the pole, positive along the incident light; here the object, image and focus are all on the same side as the incoming light, so \(PB = -u\), \(PB' = -v\) and \(PF = -f\):
\(\dfrac{(-v) - (-f)}{(-f)} = \dfrac{(-v)}{(-u)}\)
\(\dfrac{v - f}{f} = \dfrac{v}{u}\)
Cross-multiplying, \(uv - uf = vf\). Dividing throughout by uvf:
\(\dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{u}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
which is the mirror formula. The sign convention is not decoration here — the formula takes this symmetric form only because u, v and f were all substituted as negative quantities, and the same derivation done with unsigned lengths produces a relation that fails for a convex mirror.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: How is the necessary force provided to an electron to keep it moving in a circular orbit according to Bohr model of hydrogen atom ? Derive an expression for the total energy of an electron moving in an orbit of radius r in hydrogen atom. Give the significance of negative sign in this expression.
rows.solution:
THE FORCE THAT KEEPS THE ELECTRON IN ORBIT. The electron is negative and the nucleus positive, so the ELECTROSTATIC FORCE OF ATTRACTION between them supplies exactly the centripetal force the circular orbit requires. For hydrogen, with \(Z = 1\):
\(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}} \qquad \ldots(1)\)
KINETIC ENERGY. Multiply equation (1) through by \(\dfrac{r}{2}\):
\(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\)
POTENTIAL ENERGY. This is the electrostatic potential energy of the two charges \(+e\) and \(-e\) separated by r, taking it as zero when they are infinitely far apart:
\(U = \dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r} = \dfrac{(+e)(-e)}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r} = -\dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\)
TOTAL ENERGY. Adding the two, over the common denominator \(8\pi\varepsilon_{0}r\):
\(E = K + U = \dfrac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}r} - \dfrac{2e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\)
\(E = -\dfrac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\)
SIGNIFICANCE OF THE NEGATIVE SIGN. It means the electron is BOUND to the nucleus. The zero of energy was chosen as the electron at rest infinitely far away, so a negative total energy says the electron in orbit has LESS energy than a free one, and an amount \(\dfrac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\) must be supplied from outside to pull it away. The atom cannot fall apart of its own accord.
Two relations are worth carrying away from the algebra. The total energy is exactly the NEGATIVE of the kinetic energy, \(E = -K\), and exactly HALF the potential energy, \(E = \dfrac{U}{2}\). Both are properties of any inverse-square attraction, gravitational orbits included.

rows.stem:
(a) Consider the so-called 'D-T reaction' (Deuterium-Tritium reaction). In a thermonuclear fusion reactor, the following nuclear reaction occurs :
\(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} + Q\)
Find the amount of energy released in the reaction.
Given :
\(m\left({}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\right) = 2{\cdot}014102\) u
\(m\left({}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\right) = 3{\cdot}016049\) u
\(m\left({}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\right) = 4{\cdot}002603\) u
\(m\left({}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}\right) = 1{\cdot}008665\) u
\(1\ \mathrm{u} = 931\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2\)
(b) Show that the nuclear density is independent of mass number.
rows.solution:
(a) ENERGY RELEASED IN THE D-T REACTION.
Energy is released because the products are LIGHTER than the reactants; the missing mass is what appears as energy.
\(\Delta m = \left[m\left(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\right) + m\left(^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\right)\right] - \left[m\left(^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\right) + m\left(^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}\right)\right]\)
\(\Delta m = \left[2{\cdot}014102 + 3{\cdot}016049\right] - \left[4{\cdot}002603 + 1{\cdot}008665\right]\)
\(\Delta m = 5{\cdot}030151 - 5{\cdot}011268\)
\(\Delta m = 0{\cdot}018883\ \mathrm{u}\)
Converting with \(1\ \mathrm{u} = 931\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}\):
\(Q = \Delta m \times 931 = 0{\cdot}018883 \times 931\)
\(Q = 17{\cdot}58\ \mathrm{MeV}\)
Carry all six decimal places through the subtraction: the two totals agree to two decimal places, so rounding the masses even slightly destroys the answer.
(b) NUCLEAR DENSITY IS INDEPENDENT OF MASS NUMBER.
A nucleus of mass number A contains A nucleons each of mass about m, so its mass is \(mA\). Its radius follows the empirical relation
\(R = R_{0}A^{1/3}\)
so treating it as a sphere,
\(\rho = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{mA}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}} = \dfrac{mA}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(R_{0}A^{1/3}\right)^{3}}\)
The cube undoes the cube root exactly, giving \(R^{3} = R_{0}^{3}A\), so
\(\rho = \dfrac{mA}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_{0}^{3}A} = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_{0}^{3}}\)
A CANCELS COMPLETELY, leaving only constants. The nuclear density is therefore the same for every nucleus, about \(2{\cdot}3 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\).
The cancellation is the whole content of \(R \propto A^{1/3}\): volume grows in exact proportion to the number of nucleons, so nucleons are packed at a fixed density and are not squeezed closer together in heavier nuclei. That is the saturation of the short-range nuclear force showing itself in the geometry.

rows.stem: Consider a capacitor of capacitance C, with plate area A and plate separation d, filled with air [Fig. (a)]. The distance between the plates is increased to 2d and one of the plates is shifted as shown in Fig. (b). The capacitance of the new system now is :
rows.context:
A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. In practice, the two conductors have charges Q and – Q with potential difference \(V = V_1 - V_2\) between them. The ratio \(\dfrac{Q}{V}\) is a constant, denoted by C and is called the capacitance of the capacitor. It is independent of Q or V. It depends only on the geometrical configuration (shape, size, separation) of the two conductors and the medium separating the conductors. When a parallel plate capacitor is charged, the electric field \(E_0\) is localised between the plates and is uniform throughout. When a slab of a dielectric is inserted between the charged plates (charge density \(\sigma\)), the dielectric is polarised by the field. Consequently opposite charges appear on the faces of the slab, near the plates, with surface charge density of magnitude \(\sigma_p\). For a linear dielectric \(\sigma_p\) is proportional to \(E_0\). Introduction of a dielectric changes the electric field, and hence, the capacitance of a capacitor, and hence, the energy stored in the capacitor.
Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series or in parallel or in a combination of series and parallel.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only that 'one of the plates is shifted as shown', so how far it is shifted exists nowhere but the drawing. What is drawn: two sketches side by side. Fig. (a) is two short vertical parallel plates, the left one labelled A, with a dashed horizontal line between them and the gap marked d. Fig. (b) is the same left plate A and a second vertical plate further right, with the gap marked 2d and the dashed line running between them. WITHHELD: the vertical offset of the shifted plate, i.e. how much of the two plates still faces each other, which is exactly what the four options discriminate. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
TWO things change at once, and each one on its own would halve the capacitance.
The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor is
\(C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}\)
FIRST, the separation is doubled from d to 2d, which halves C.
SECOND, one plate is SHIFTED sideways, so the plates no longer face each other completely. Only the OVERLAPPING part of the plates forms a capacitor — field lines exist only where one plate faces the other — and from figure (b) the overlap is half the plate area. So the effective area is \(\dfrac{A}{2}\), which halves C again.
Putting both together:
\(C' = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}{2d} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}\right)\)
\(C' = \dfrac{C}{4}\)
The new capacitance is \(\dfrac{C}{4}\).
The shift is easy to overlook, since the stem mentions it only as "one of the plates is shifted as shown" and gives no number — the figure carries it. A reader who accounts for the doubled separation alone arrives at \(\dfrac{C}{2}\), which is offered.

rows.stem: A slab (area A and thickness \(d_1\)) of a linear dielectric of dielectric constant K is inserted between charged plates (charge density \(\sigma\)) of a parallel plate capacitor [plate area A and plate separation \(d\ (> d_1)\)] and opposite charges with charge density of magnitude \(\sigma_p\) appear on the faces of the slab. The dielectric constant K is given by :
rows.context:
A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. In practice, the two conductors have charges Q and – Q with potential difference \(V = V_1 - V_2\) between them. The ratio \(\dfrac{Q}{V}\) is a constant, denoted by C and is called the capacitance of the capacitor. It is independent of Q or V. It depends only on the geometrical configuration (shape, size, separation) of the two conductors and the medium separating the conductors. When a parallel plate capacitor is charged, the electric field \(E_0\) is localised between the plates and is uniform throughout. When a slab of a dielectric is inserted between the charged plates (charge density \(\sigma\)), the dielectric is polarised by the field. Consequently opposite charges appear on the faces of the slab, near the plates, with surface charge density of magnitude \(\sigma_p\). For a linear dielectric \(\sigma_p\) is proportional to \(E_0\). Introduction of a dielectric changes the electric field, and hence, the capacitance of a capacitor, and hence, the energy stored in the capacitor.
Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series or in parallel or in a combination of series and parallel.
rows.solution:
Inside the dielectric two opposing fields exist at once, and K is defined by how much the second one cuts the first down.
The free charge on the plates, of surface density \(\sigma\), sets up a field
\(E_{0} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
The polarised dielectric develops bound charges of surface density \(\sigma_{p}\) on its faces, with the sign opposite to the neighbouring plate. These produce their OWN field opposing the first:
\(E_{p} = \dfrac{\sigma_{p}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
The net field inside the slab is the difference:
\(E = E_{0} - E_{p} = \dfrac{\sigma - \sigma_{p}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
The dielectric constant is defined as the factor by which the dielectric reduces the field:
\(K = \dfrac{E_{0}}{E} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}}}{\dfrac{\sigma - \sigma_{p}}{\varepsilon_{0}}}\)
\(K = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sigma - \sigma_{p}}\)
Check the two limits. With no polarisation, \(\sigma_{p} = 0\) and \(K = 1\), which is vacuum. As \(\sigma_{p} \to \sigma\) the denominator vanishes and \(K \to \infty\), which is a conductor — its induced charges cancel the field completely. Every real dielectric sits between, so the bound charge density is always LESS than the free charge density, and K is finite and greater than 1.

rows.stem: An electric field E is established between the plates of an air filled parallel plate capacitor, with charges Q and – Q. V is the volume of the space enclosed between the plates. The energy stored in the capacitor is :
rows.context:
A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. In practice, the two conductors have charges Q and – Q with potential difference \(V = V_1 - V_2\) between them. The ratio \(\dfrac{Q}{V}\) is a constant, denoted by C and is called the capacitance of the capacitor. It is independent of Q or V. It depends only on the geometrical configuration (shape, size, separation) of the two conductors and the medium separating the conductors. When a parallel plate capacitor is charged, the electric field \(E_0\) is localised between the plates and is uniform throughout. When a slab of a dielectric is inserted between the charged plates (charge density \(\sigma\)), the dielectric is polarised by the field. Consequently opposite charges appear on the faces of the slab, near the plates, with surface charge density of magnitude \(\sigma_p\). For a linear dielectric \(\sigma_p\) is proportional to \(E_0\). Introduction of a dielectric changes the electric field, and hence, the capacitance of a capacitor, and hence, the energy stored in the capacitor.
Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series or in parallel or in a combination of series and parallel.
rows.solution:
The energy of a charged capacitor can be thought of as residing in the electric FIELD between the plates, with an energy per unit volume, or energy density, of
\(u = \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{0}E^{2}\)
Since the field here is uniform throughout the enclosed space, the total energy is just this density multiplied by the volume V it occupies:
\(U = uV\)
\(U = \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{0}E^{2}V\)
The energy stored is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{0}E^{2}V\).
Dimensions settle this even without recalling the formula. The option \(\dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{0}E^{2}\) is an energy per unit VOLUME, not an energy, so it cannot be the answer to a question asking for the energy stored — it needs the volume factor the stem deliberately supplies. The remaining two options mix Q and E together, which double-counts: the field E is already produced BY the charge Q, so a correct expression uses one or the other, not both.
The same energy is of course \(\dfrac{1}{2}CV^{2} = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C}\). Writing it as a field energy is what lets the idea survive beyond capacitors: the energy density \(\dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{0}E^{2}\) applies to any electric field, including the one carried by a light wave.

rows.stem: Three capacitors A, B and M, each of capacitance C are connected to a capacitor N of capacitance 2C and a battery as shown in the figure. If the charges on A and N are Q and \(Q'\) respectively, then \(\dfrac{Q'}{Q}\) is :
rows.context:
A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. In practice, the two conductors have charges Q and – Q with potential difference \(V = V_1 - V_2\) between them. The ratio \(\dfrac{Q}{V}\) is a constant, denoted by C and is called the capacitance of the capacitor. It is independent of Q or V. It depends only on the geometrical configuration (shape, size, separation) of the two conductors and the medium separating the conductors. When a parallel plate capacitor is charged, the electric field \(E_0\) is localised between the plates and is uniform throughout. When a slab of a dielectric is inserted between the charged plates (charge density \(\sigma\)), the dielectric is polarised by the field. Consequently opposite charges appear on the faces of the slab, near the plates, with surface charge density of magnitude \(\sigma_p\). For a linear dielectric \(\sigma_p\) is proportional to \(E_0\). Introduction of a dielectric changes the electric field, and hence, the capacitance of a capacitor, and hence, the energy stored in the capacitor.
Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series or in parallel or in a combination of series and parallel.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem names the four capacitors and the battery but not how they are wired, and the ratio asked for depends entirely on that. What can safely be said about the layout: the circuit is drawn as a rectangle, with capacitor A in the top side, capacitors B and M in the left and right vertical sides respectively, capacitor N in a horizontal branch across the middle and the battery, labelled V, in the bottom side. WITHHELD: nothing further — the plate orientations and the exact node joins are left to the drawing, and the series/parallel grouping that follows from them is the answer. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
Read the wiring off the figure first, because the question is entirely about which capacitors are in series and which are in parallel.
The battery V is connected between the left node and the right node of the middle branch. Between those same two nodes there are TWO paths:
PATH 1: capacitor N alone, of capacitance 2C.
PATH 2: from the left node UP through B, across the top through A, and DOWN through M to the right node. So A, B and M lie in SERIES.
For the series branch:
\(\dfrac{1}{C_{s}} = \dfrac{1}{C} + \dfrac{1}{C} + \dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{3}{C} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_{s} = \dfrac{C}{3}\)
Both paths are connected directly across the battery, so both carry the same potential difference V.
CHARGE ON A. Capacitors in series all carry the SAME charge, so the charge on A is the charge on the whole series branch:
\(Q = C_{s}V = \dfrac{C}{3}V\)
CHARGE ON N:
\(Q' = 2CV\)
Taking the ratio, and cancelling CV:
\(\dfrac{Q'}{Q} = \dfrac{2CV}{\dfrac{C}{3}V} = 2 \times 3\)
\(\dfrac{Q'}{Q} = 6\)
The ratio is 6.
Two separate factors of the answer are worth separating: N is twice the capacitance of any single capacitor, and the series chain is only a third of one. The reciprocal \(\dfrac{1}{6}\) is offered for a reader who takes the ratio the other way round, and 3 for one who forgets that N is 2C rather than C.

rows.stem: A slab (area A and thickness \(\dfrac{d}{2}\)) of dielectric constant K is inserted in a parallel plate capacitor of plate area A and plate separation d. If C and \(C_0\) are the capacitances of the capacitors with and without the dielectric, then \(\dfrac{C}{C_0}\) is :
rows.context:
A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator. In practice, the two conductors have charges Q and – Q with potential difference \(V = V_1 - V_2\) between them. The ratio \(\dfrac{Q}{V}\) is a constant, denoted by C and is called the capacitance of the capacitor. It is independent of Q or V. It depends only on the geometrical configuration (shape, size, separation) of the two conductors and the medium separating the conductors. When a parallel plate capacitor is charged, the electric field \(E_0\) is localised between the plates and is uniform throughout. When a slab of a dielectric is inserted between the charged plates (charge density \(\sigma\)), the dielectric is polarised by the field. Consequently opposite charges appear on the faces of the slab, near the plates, with surface charge density of magnitude \(\sigma_p\). For a linear dielectric \(\sigma_p\) is proportional to \(E_0\). Introduction of a dielectric changes the electric field, and hence, the capacitance of a capacitor, and hence, the energy stored in the capacitor.
Like resistors, capacitors can also be arranged in series or in parallel or in a combination of series and parallel.
rows.solution:
The slab fills only half the gap, so the space between the plates is TWO capacitors in series: a thickness \(\dfrac{d}{2}\) of dielectric and a thickness \(\dfrac{d}{2}\) of air.
Without the dielectric:
\(C_{0} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}\)
The dielectric-filled half, of thickness \(\dfrac{d}{2}\):
\(C_{1} = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_{0}A}{d/2} = \dfrac{2K\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}\)
The air-filled half, of the same thickness:
\(C_{2} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d/2} = \dfrac{2\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}\)
They are in SERIES, because the same field lines pass through one and then the other:
\(\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{C_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{C_{2}} = \dfrac{d}{2K\varepsilon_{0}A} + \dfrac{d}{2\varepsilon_{0}A} = \dfrac{d}{2\varepsilon_{0}A}\left(\dfrac{1}{K} + 1\right) = \dfrac{d}{2\varepsilon_{0}A} \times \dfrac{1 + K}{K}\)
Inverting:
\(C = \dfrac{2K\varepsilon_{0}A}{d(K + 1)}\)
Dividing by \(C_{0}\), so that \(\dfrac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}\) cancels:
\(\dfrac{C}{C_{0}} = \dfrac{2K}{K + 1}\)
Two checks. With \(K = 1\) the slab is not a dielectric at all and the ratio gives \(\dfrac{2}{2} = 1\), correctly leaving the capacitor unchanged. For large K the ratio tends to 2, not to K — filling only half the gap can never more than double the capacitance, however good the dielectric, because the empty half still contributes its own series capacitance and limits the whole.

rows.stem: Which of the following is a donor impurity atom for Ge ?
rows.context: Extrinsic semiconductors are made by doping pure or intrinsic semiconductors with suitable impurity. There are two type of dopants used in doping, Si or Ge, and using them p-type and n-type semiconductors can be obtained. A p-n junction is the basic building block of many semiconductor devices. Two important processes occur during the formation of a p-n junction : diffusion and drift. When such a junction is formed, a 'depletion layer' is created consisting of immobile ion-cores. This is responsible for a junction potential barrier. The width of a depletion layer and the height of potential barrier changes when a junction is forward-biased or reverse-biased. A semiconductor diode is basically a p-n junction with metallic contacts provided at the ends for application of an external voltage. Using diodes, alternating voltages can be rectified.
rows.solution:
Germanium is TETRAVALENT, so a donor impurity must be PENTAVALENT. Four of its five valence electrons complete the covalent bonds with the neighbouring Ge atoms, and the fifth is left over — loosely bound to its parent atom and easily freed into the conduction band, where it DONATES an electron to the crystal.
Checking the four candidates against the periodic table:
Boron, aluminium and indium are all in GROUP 13 and are TRIVALENT. Each leaves one bond incomplete, creating a hole, so all three are ACCEPTOR impurities producing p-type material.
Antimony is in GROUP 15 and is PENTAVALENT, so it is the donor.
So antimony is the donor impurity atom for Ge.
Three of the four options being acceptors is the shape of the question: the work is recognising the group of each element, not recalling the definition. The other common pentavalent dopants are phosphorus, arsenic and bismuth.

rows.stem: When a pentavalent atom occupies the position of an atom in the crystal lattice of Si, four of its electrons form covalent bonds with four silicon neighbours, while the fifth remains bound to the parent atom. The energy required to set this electron free is about :
rows.context: Extrinsic semiconductors are made by doping pure or intrinsic semiconductors with suitable impurity. There are two type of dopants used in doping, Si or Ge, and using them p-type and n-type semiconductors can be obtained. A p-n junction is the basic building block of many semiconductor devices. Two important processes occur during the formation of a p-n junction : diffusion and drift. When such a junction is formed, a 'depletion layer' is created consisting of immobile ion-cores. This is responsible for a junction potential barrier. The width of a depletion layer and the height of potential barrier changes when a junction is forward-biased or reverse-biased. A semiconductor diode is basically a p-n junction with metallic contacts provided at the ends for application of an external voltage. Using diodes, alternating voltages can be rectified.
rows.solution:
The fifth electron of a pentavalent donor is not in a covalent bond — the four bonds are already complete — so nothing holds it but the weak residual attraction of its own parent ion, screened by the surrounding silicon lattice.
That binding is far weaker than a covalent bond, and the energy needed to set the electron free is correspondingly small:
about \(0{\cdot}05\ \mathrm{eV}\) for silicon (and around \(0{\cdot}01\) eV for germanium).
Compare this with the energy needed to break a covalent bond in silicon, which is the band gap \(E_{g} \approx 1{\cdot}1\) eV — more than twenty times larger. Compare it also with the average thermal energy available at room temperature, about \(kT \approx 0{\cdot}026\) eV.
That comparison is the point of the number. At room temperature there is enough thermal energy to ionise essentially EVERY donor atom, while only a tiny fraction of covalent bonds break. This is exactly why doping works: a trace of impurity, one part in millions, can raise the conductivity enormously, because all of its electrons are released while the host contributes almost none. On a band diagram the donor level sits just \(0{\cdot}05\) eV below the bottom of the conduction band.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: During formation of a p-n junction :
rows.context: Extrinsic semiconductors are made by doping pure or intrinsic semiconductors with suitable impurity. There are two type of dopants used in doping, Si or Ge, and using them p-type and n-type semiconductors can be obtained. A p-n junction is the basic building block of many semiconductor devices. Two important processes occur during the formation of a p-n junction : diffusion and drift. When such a junction is formed, a 'depletion layer' is created consisting of immobile ion-cores. This is responsible for a junction potential barrier. The width of a depletion layer and the height of potential barrier changes when a junction is forward-biased or reverse-biased. A semiconductor diode is basically a p-n junction with metallic contacts provided at the ends for application of an external voltage. Using diodes, alternating voltages can be rectified.

options.label: A
options.text: a layer of negative charge on n-side and a layer of positive charge on p-side appear.

options.label: B
options.text: a layer of positive charge on n-side and a layer of negative charge on p-side appear.

options.label: C
options.text: the electrons on p-side of the junction move to n-side initially.

options.label: D
options.text: initially diffusion current is small and drift current is large.

rows.solution:
When a p-n junction forms, electrons DIFFUSE from the n-side, where they are plentiful, into the p-side, and holes diffuse the opposite way. The question is what they leave behind.
An electron leaving the n-side leaves behind its parent DONOR ION, which is positively charged and, being part of the crystal lattice, IMMOBILE. So a layer of POSITIVE charge builds up on the n-side of the junction.
A hole leaving the p-side leaves behind a negatively charged ACCEPTOR ION, equally immobile, so a layer of NEGATIVE charge builds up on the p-side.
So during formation a layer of positive charge appears on the n side and a layer of negative charge on the p side.
Two of the other options can be dismissed directly. Electrons on the p-side are MINORITY carriers and are far too few to drive the process, so it is not they who move to the n-side initially. And the diffusion current is LARGE at the start while the drift current is small — the drift current only grows as the field builds up, until the two balance and the junction reaches equilibrium.
Note the direction of the resulting field: it runs from the positive n-side to the negative p-side, which is precisely the direction that OPPOSES further diffusion. That self-limiting field is the barrier potential.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: In reverse-biased p-n junction :
rows.context: Extrinsic semiconductors are made by doping pure or intrinsic semiconductors with suitable impurity. There are two type of dopants used in doping, Si or Ge, and using them p-type and n-type semiconductors can be obtained. A p-n junction is the basic building block of many semiconductor devices. Two important processes occur during the formation of a p-n junction : diffusion and drift. When such a junction is formed, a 'depletion layer' is created consisting of immobile ion-cores. This is responsible for a junction potential barrier. The width of a depletion layer and the height of potential barrier changes when a junction is forward-biased or reverse-biased. A semiconductor diode is basically a p-n junction with metallic contacts provided at the ends for application of an external voltage. Using diodes, alternating voltages can be rectified.

options.label: A
options.text: the drift current is of the order of few mA.

options.label: B
options.text: the applied voltage mostly drops across the depletion region.

options.label: D
options.text: the current increases with increase in applied voltage.

rows.solution:
In reverse bias the applied voltage adds to the built-in potential, widening the depletion region and raising the barrier.
Where that voltage appears is a question of resistance. The p-region and the n-region are doped and full of mobile carriers, so their resistance is low, of the order of ohms. The DEPLETION REGION has been swept clear of mobile carriers altogether and is effectively an insulator, with a resistance running into megohms.
Resistances in series share a voltage in proportion to their size, so almost all of the applied voltage drops across the depletion region and almost none across the neutral regions.
So in a reverse-biased junction the applied voltage mostly drops across the depletion region.
Each of the other three statements is false, and for a distinct reason. The depletion width INCREASES under reverse bias, not decreases. The reverse current is carried by MINORITY carriers, of which there are very few, so it is of the order of microamperes, not milliamperes. And it barely rises with voltage at all — the reverse characteristic is flat, because the current is limited by how many minority carriers are thermally generated, not by how hard they are pulled.
