rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem: The output frequency of a full-wave rectifier with 50 Hz as input frequency is :
rows.context: Extrinsic semiconductors are made by doping pure or intrinsic semiconductors with suitable impurity. There are two type of dopants used in doping, Si or Ge, and using them p-type and n-type semiconductors can be obtained. A p-n junction is the basic building block of many semiconductor devices. Two important processes occur during the formation of a p-n junction : diffusion and drift. When such a junction is formed, a 'depletion layer' is created consisting of immobile ion-cores. This is responsible for a junction potential barrier. The width of a depletion layer and the height of potential barrier changes when a junction is forward-biased or reverse-biased. A semiconductor diode is basically a p-n junction with metallic contacts provided at the ends for application of an external voltage. Using diodes, alternating voltages can be rectified.
rows.solution:
A HALF-wave rectifier passes only one half of each input cycle, so its output pulses at the input frequency, 50 Hz.
A FULL-wave rectifier uses both halves. The positive half cycles pass through unchanged, and the negative half cycles are FLIPPED UP rather than discarded, so a hump appears in the output for EACH half cycle of the input.
Two humps per input cycle means the output repeats twice as often:
\(f_{out} = 2 \times f_{in} = 2 \times 50\)
\(f_{out} = 100\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
The output frequency is 100 Hz.
This doubling is the practical advantage of full-wave rectification, and not only because no energy is thrown away. The gaps between successive humps are half as long, so the output is closer to steady and a smoothing capacitor has less time to discharge between them — giving a smaller ripple for the same capacitor. The distractor 50 Hz is the half-wave answer, and 25 Hz would require the output to repeat half as often as the input, which nothing in a rectifier does.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the principle of working of an ac generator. Draw its labelled diagram and explain its working.
(ii) A resistor of 400 \(\Omega\), an inductor of \(\left(\dfrac{5}{\pi}\right)\)H and a capacitor of \(\left(\dfrac{50}{\pi}\right)\mu\mathrm{F}\) are joined in series across an ac source \(v = 140 \sin (100\pi)t\) V. Find the rms voltages across these three circuit elements. The algebraic sum of these voltages is more than the rms voltage of source. Explain.
rows.solution:
(i) PRINCIPLE, DIAGRAM AND WORKING OF AN AC GENERATOR.
PRINCIPLE. It works on the principle of ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION: when the magnetic flux linked with a coil changes, an emf is induced in it.
DIAGRAM. Draw a rectangular coil mounted on an axle between the poles of a magnet, N on one side and S on the other. The two ends of the coil are connected to two separate SLIP RINGS, against which two carbon BRUSHES press, and the brushes lead to the external circuit. Label the coil, the axle, the pole pieces, the slip rings, the carbon brushes and the alternating emf output.
WORKING. The coil is rotated mechanically in the uniform field. As it turns, the angle between the field and the normal to the coil changes continuously, so the flux linked with it changes and an emf is induced. With the coil of N turns and area A rotating at angular velocity \(\omega\) in a field B,
\(\phi = NBA\cos\omega t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t\)
The emf is greatest when the coil's plane is PARALLEL to the field, since the flux is then changing fastest, and zero when the plane is perpendicular to it. Every half revolution the coil's faces exchange places relative to the poles, so the induced emf REVERSES direction — which is what makes the output alternating. The slip rings, being continuous rings, keep each coil end connected to its own brush throughout, so this reversal is carried out to the circuit unchanged.
(ii) THE SERIES LCR CIRCUIT.
From \(v = 140\sin(100\pi t)\): \(V_{0} = 140\) V and \(\omega = 100\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).
REACTANCES:
\(X_{L} = \omega L = 100\pi \times \dfrac{5}{\pi} = 500\ \Omega\)
\(X_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{100\pi \times \dfrac{50}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{10^{6}}{100 \times 50} = 200\ \Omega\)
IMPEDANCE:
\(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_{L} - X_{C})^{2}} = \sqrt{(400)^{2} + (300)^{2}} = \sqrt{250000} = 500\ \Omega\)
RMS CURRENT, the same through all three since they are in series:
\(I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{140}{\sqrt{2} \times 500} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}28}{\sqrt{2}}\ \mathrm{A}\)
RMS VOLTAGES:
\(\left(V_{rms}\right)_{R} = I_{rms}R = \dfrac{0{\cdot}28}{\sqrt{2}} \times 400 = \dfrac{112}{\sqrt{2}} = 56\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{V} \approx 79\ \mathrm{V}\)
\(\left(V_{rms}\right)_{L} = I_{rms}X_{L} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}28}{\sqrt{2}} \times 500 = \dfrac{140}{\sqrt{2}} = 70\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{V} \approx 99\ \mathrm{V}\)
\(\left(V_{rms}\right)_{C} = I_{rms}X_{C} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}28}{\sqrt{2}} \times 200 = \dfrac{56}{\sqrt{2}} = 28\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{V} \approx 40\ \mathrm{V}\)
WHY THE SUM EXCEEDS THE SOURCE VOLTAGE. Adding them arithmetically gives \(154\sqrt{2} \approx 218\) V, while the source is only \(\dfrac{140}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 99\) V. Nothing is wrong: the three voltages are NOT IN PHASE, so they never reach their maxima at the same instant and cannot simply be added.
They must be combined as phasors. \(V_{R}\) is in phase with the current, \(V_{L}\) leads it by \(90^{\circ}\) and \(V_{C}\) LAGS it by \(90^{\circ}\), so \(V_{L}\) and \(V_{C}\) are in direct opposition and partly cancel before either meets \(V_{R}\):
\(V = \sqrt{V_{R}^{2} + \left(V_{L} - V_{C}\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{\left(56\sqrt{2}\right)^{2} + \left(42\sqrt{2}\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{56^{2} + 42^{2}} = 70\sqrt{2} \approx 99\ \mathrm{V}\)
which is exactly the source voltage, as it must be.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the principle of working of a transformer. With the help of a labelled diagram, explain the working of a step-up transformer.
(ii) An ideal transformer is designed to convert 50 V into 250 V. It draws 200 W power from an ac source whose instantaneous voltage is given by \(v_i = 20 \sin (100\pi)t\) V.
Find :
(I) rms value of input current.
(II) expression for instantaneous output voltage.
(III) expression for instantaneous output current.
rows.solution:
(i) PRINCIPLE, DIAGRAM AND WORKING OF A STEP-UP TRANSFORMER.
PRINCIPLE. It works on the principle of MUTUAL INDUCTION: an alternating current in one coil induces an emf in a neighbouring coil linked to it by a common magnetic flux.
DIAGRAM. Draw a closed rectangular core of LAMINATED SOFT IRON. Wind the PRIMARY of \(N_{P}\) turns on one limb and connect it to the ac input. Wind the SECONDARY of \(N_{S}\) turns on the other limb and take the output from it. For a step-up transformer \(N_{S} > N_{P}\). Label the core, both windings and the input and output terminals.
WORKING. The alternating voltage applied to the primary drives an alternating current, which sets up an alternating magnetic flux in the core. The core is a closed magnetic circuit of high permeability, so it carries essentially ALL of that flux through the secondary as well, and each turn of either winding links the SAME flux \(\phi\).
The emf induced in a winding is proportional to its number of turns:
\(\varepsilon_{S} = -N_{S}\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} \qquad \varepsilon_{P} = -N_{P}\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\)
Dividing, the common \(\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\) cancels and leaves
\(\dfrac{v_{S}}{v_{P}} = \dfrac{N_{S}}{N_{P}}\)
Since the secondary has MORE turns, a larger emf is developed across it, and the voltage is stepped up.
(ii) THE NUMERICAL PARTS.
From \(v_{i} = 20\sin(100\pi t)\): peak input \(20\) V, so \(\left(V_{i}\right)_{rms} = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt{2}}\) V. The turns ratio comes from the design specification, \(50\) V converted to \(250\) V:
\(\dfrac{V_{o}}{V_{i}} = \dfrac{250}{50} = 5\)
(I) RMS VALUE OF INPUT CURRENT. The transformer draws 200 W from the source:
\(P_{i} = \left(V_{i}\right)_{rms}\left(I_{P}\right)_{rms} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 200 = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt{2}} \times I_{P}\)
\(I_{P} = \dfrac{200\sqrt{2}}{20} = 10\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{A} \approx 14{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{A}\)
(II) INSTANTANEOUS OUTPUT VOLTAGE. The turns ratio multiplies the whole waveform, instant by instant, so the shape and frequency are unchanged and only the amplitude scales:
\(v_{o} = 5 \times 20\sin(100\pi t)\)
\(v_{o} = 100\sin(100\pi t)\ \mathrm{V}\)
(III) INSTANTANEOUS OUTPUT CURRENT. For an ideal transformer the output power equals the input power:
\(P_{o} = \left(V_{o}\right)_{rms}\left(I_{o}\right)_{rms} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 200 = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{2}} \times \left(I_{o}\right)_{rms}\)
\(\left(I_{o}\right)_{rms} = 2\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{A}\)
The peak is \(\sqrt{2}\) times the rms, so
\(I_{o} = \left(2\sqrt{2}\right)\sqrt{2}\sin(100\pi t)\)
\(I_{o} = 4\sin(100\pi t)\ \mathrm{A}\)
The voltage has been stepped up five times and the current stepped DOWN five times, from \(10\sqrt{2}\) A to \(2\sqrt{2}\) A. Nothing has been created: the transformer trades voltage for current, and the product of the two is the same on both sides.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram to show the image formation by a compound microscope. Obtain the expression for the total magnification of the microscope when the final image is formed at infinity.
(ii) In a compound microscope, an object is placed at a distance of \(1{\cdot}5\) cm from the objective of focal length \(1{\cdot}25\) cm. The eyepiece has a focal length of 5 cm. The final image is formed at infinity. Calculate the distance between the objective and the eyepiece.
rows.solution:
(i) RAY DIAGRAM AND TOTAL MAGNIFICATION OF A COMPOUND MICROSCOPE.
RAY DIAGRAM. Draw two converging lenses on a common axis: the OBJECTIVE of short focal length \(f_{o}\) and small aperture, and the EYEPIECE of focal length \(f_{e}\). Place the object AB just BEYOND the objective's focus, so the objective forms a real, inverted, magnified image \(A'B'\) inside the tube. Position the eyepiece so that \(A'B'\) falls at its focus, and the final image \(A''B''\) is then formed at INFINITY, inverted with respect to the object. Mark \(f_{o}\), \(f_{e}\), the tube length L and the near-point distance D, with arrows on every ray.
MAGNIFICATION BY THE OBJECTIVE. Taking the image distance as the tube length L,
\(m_{o} = \dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{L}{f_{o}}\)
MAGNIFICATION BY THE EYEPIECE. Used as a simple magnifier it gives \(m_{e} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\) in general, but when the final image is at INFINITY the intermediate image sits exactly at its focus and
\(m_{e} = \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\)
TOTAL MAGNIFICATION. The eyepiece magnifies what the objective has already produced, so the two multiply:
\(m = m_{o} \times m_{e} = \left(\dfrac{L}{f_{o}}\right)\left(\dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\right)\)
Both focal lengths are in the denominator, which is why a microscope needs BOTH lenses to be of short focal length — the opposite of a telescope, whose objective must be long.
(ii) THE SEPARATION OF THE LENSES.
First locate the image formed by the objective, using \(u_{o} = -1{\cdot}5\) cm and \(f_{o} = 1{\cdot}25\) cm:
\(\dfrac{1}{v_{o}} - \dfrac{1}{u_{o}} = \dfrac{1}{f_{o}}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{v_{o}} - \dfrac{1}{(-1{\cdot}5)} = \dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}25}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{v_{o}} = \dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}25} - \dfrac{1}{1{\cdot}5} = 0{\cdot}8 - 0{\cdot}667 = 0{\cdot}1333\)
\(v_{o} = 7{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The final image is at infinity, so this intermediate image must lie exactly at the eyepiece's focus, a distance \(f_{e}\) in front of it:
\(L = |v_{o}| + |f_{e}| = 7{\cdot}5 + 5\)
\(L = 12{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The objective and the eyepiece must be 12.5 cm apart.
Note how little room there is to spare: the object sits at 1.5 cm against a focal length of 1.25 cm, only a quarter of a centimetre beyond the focus. That is what produces the objective's magnification of five, and it is why a microscope must be focused so delicately.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem:
(i) Using Huygens' principle, explain the refraction of a plane wavefront, propagating in air, at a plane interface between air and glass. Hence verify Snell's law.
(ii) Use mirror formula to deduce that a convex mirror always produces a virtual image of an object kept in front of it.
rows.solution:
(i) REFRACTION OF A PLANE WAVEFRONT, AND SNELL'S LAW.
Let a plane wavefront AB travelling in air at speed \(v_{1}\) strike the plane surface of glass at an angle i, reaching the surface first at A. The far end B has still to travel the distance BC to reach the surface. If that takes a time \(\tau\), then
\(BC = v_{1}\tau\)
During the SAME time \(\tau\), the secondary wavelet that started at A has been spreading INTO the glass, where the speed is \(v_{2}\), so it has travelled only
\(AE = v_{2}\tau\)
and since \(v_{2} < v_{1}\) it has not got as far. Draw a sphere of radius \(v_{2}\tau\) centred on A, and the tangent to it from C. That tangent CE is the REFRACTED WAVEFRONT, and the refracted rays are perpendicular to it, making an angle r with the normal.
Now use the two right-angled triangles on the common hypotenuse AC:
\(\sin i = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{v_{1}\tau}{AC} \qquad\qquad \sin r = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{v_{2}\tau}{AC}\)
Dividing, and cancelling both AC and \(\tau\):
\(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}\)
Writing each speed in terms of the refractive index, \(v_{1} = \dfrac{c}{n_{1}}\) and \(v_{2} = \dfrac{c}{n_{2}}\):
\(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{c/n_{1}}{c/n_{2}} = \dfrac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n_{1}\sin i = n_{2}\sin r\)
which is Snell's law. The bending is thus explained physically: the wavefront pivots because one end of it enters the slower medium before the other.
(ii) A CONVEX MIRROR ALWAYS GIVES A VIRTUAL IMAGE.
Start from the mirror formula:
\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
Apply the sign convention. For a real object placed in front of the mirror, \(u\) is NEGATIVE. For a CONVEX mirror the focus lies BEHIND the mirror, so \(f\) is POSITIVE. Substituting \(u \to -u\) with u now a positive number:
\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{(-u)} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u}\)
Both terms on the right are POSITIVE — the first because f is positive for a convex mirror, the second because u is a positive number — so their sum is positive:
\(\dfrac{1}{v} \ \text{is positive} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v \ \text{is positive}\)
A positive v means the image lies BEHIND the mirror, where no light actually reaches, so the image is VIRTUAL.
Nothing in the argument depended on the value of u, which is what makes the conclusion unconditional: however near or far the object is placed, \(\dfrac{1}{f}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{u}\) are both positive and cannot cancel. A convex mirror can never form a real image of a real object, which is precisely why it is used as a rear-view mirror — the image is always erect, diminished and visible.

rows.subtopic: Electrostatic Potential due to Charges and Dipoles
rows.stem:
(i) The electric field in a region is given by \(\vec{E} = 40x\,\hat{i}\) N/C. Find the amount of work done in taking a unit positive charge from a point (0, 3m) to the point (5m, 0).
(ii) A charge Q is distributed over two concentric hollow spheres of radii r and R (> r) such that their surface charge densities are equal. Find :
(I) the electric field, and
(II) the potential
at their common centre.
rows.solution:
(i) WORK DONE IN MOVING THE CHARGE.
The field is non-uniform, varying with x, so the potential must be obtained by integration rather than by multiplying E by a distance:
\(V = -\int \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r} = -\int 40x\,dx\)
\(V = -20x^{2}\)
The field has only an \(\hat{i}\) component, so the potential depends on x ALONE — moving in the y direction changes nothing.
At the point \(A(0, 3\ \mathrm{m})\), where \(x = 0\):
\(V_{A} = -20(0)^{2} = 0\)
At the point \(B(5\ \mathrm{m}, 0)\), where \(x = 5\):
\(V_{B} = -20(5)^{2} = -500\ \mathrm{V}\)
The work done in carrying a charge q from A to B is
\(W = q\left(V_{B} - V_{A}\right) = 1 \times (-500 - 0)\)
\(W = -500\ \mathrm{J}\)
The work done is \(-500\) J. The negative sign says the FIELD does the work, not the external agent: a positive charge moves from higher to lower potential of its own accord, so it must be held back rather than pushed.
Note that the answer depends only on the endpoints, not on the route taken — the electrostatic field is conservative, which is why the y-coordinates of A and B never entered the calculation.
(ii) THE TWO CONCENTRIC SHELLS.
(I) ELECTRIC FIELD AT THE COMMON CENTRE.
Apply Gauss's law to a small spherical surface drawn INSIDE the inner shell. All the charge lies on the two shells, both outside this surface, so the charge enclosed is zero:
\(q_{enclosed} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \phi_{E} = \oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E = 0\)
The field at the common centre is ZERO. This holds however the charge divides between the two shells — a charged spherical shell produces no field anywhere inside itself.
(II) POTENTIAL AT THE COMMON CENTRE.
Potential, unlike field, does NOT vanish inside a shell: it stays constant at its surface value. So the centre is at the surface potential of each shell, and the two contributions ADD.
First split the charge. Let the inner shell of radius r carry q and the outer of radius R carry \(Q - q\). The surface densities are equal:
\(\dfrac{q}{4\pi r^{2}} = \dfrac{Q - q}{4\pi R^{2}}\)
\(qR^{2} = (Q - q)r^{2} = Qr^{2} - qr^{2}\)
\(q\left(R^{2} + r^{2}\right) = Qr^{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q = \dfrac{Qr^{2}}{R^{2} + r^{2}}\)
By the same symmetry, \(Q - q = \dfrac{QR^{2}}{R^{2} + r^{2}}\).
Now add the two potentials at the centre, each shell contributing \(\dfrac{k \times \text{charge}}{\text{its own radius}}\):
\(V = \dfrac{kq}{r} + \dfrac{k(Q - q)}{R} = \dfrac{k}{r}\cdot\dfrac{Qr^{2}}{R^{2} + r^{2}} + \dfrac{k}{R}\cdot\dfrac{QR^{2}}{R^{2} + r^{2}}\)
\(V = \dfrac{kQr}{R^{2} + r^{2}} + \dfrac{kQR}{R^{2} + r^{2}}\)
\(V = \dfrac{kQ(R + r)}{R^{2} + r^{2}} = \dfrac{Q(R + r)}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}\left(R^{2} + r^{2}\right)}\)
The two parts together make the standard point: zero field and non-zero potential are perfectly consistent, because the field is the RATE OF CHANGE of potential. The potential inside is constant, and a constant has zero derivative.

rows.subtopic: Electric Dipole and Dipole in a Uniform Field
rows.stem:
(i) Obtain an expression for the electric field \(\vec{E}\) due to a dipole of dipole moment \(\vec{p}\) at a point on its equatorial plane and specify its direction. Hence, find the value of electric field :
(I) at the centre of the dipole (r = 0), and
(II) at a point r >> a,
where 2a is the length of the dipole.
(ii) An electric field \(\vec{E} = (10x + 5)\hat{i}\) N/C exists in a region in which a cube of side L is kept as shown in the figure. Here x and L are in metres. Calculate the net flux through the cube.
rows.figureNote:
REQUIRED — part (ii)'s flux depends on WHERE the cube sits relative to the origin, because the field varies with x, and the stem says only 'as shown in the figure'. What is drawn: a set of three axes labelled X (to the right), Y (upward) and Z (towards the lower left), with a cube of side L drawn in perspective having one vertex at the origin O. The visible vertices are labelled A, B, C and D on the upper face and its left edge, and \(A_1\), \(C_1\) and \(D_1\) on the lower face, with O between \(A_1\) and \(C_1\); the unit vector \(\hat{i}\) is marked as a short arrow along the +X direction near \(C_1\). WITHHELD: nothing further is needed — the two faces perpendicular to X and their x-coordinates are what the calculation turns on and follow from the placement above. Page idx 30.

SPLIT CHAPTER NOTE: part (i) is the dipole field (Electric Charges and Fields) and part (ii) is Gauss-law flux through a cube (Electric Charges and Fields / 'Electric Flux and Gauss's Law'), so both parts sit in the same chapter; filed on the dipole subtopic, which carries the larger share of the marks.
rows.solution:
(i) FIELD ON THE EQUATORIAL PLANE OF A DIPOLE.
Let the dipole consist of \(-q\) at A and \(+q\) at B, separated by \(2a\), and let P be a point on the equatorial plane at distance r from the centre. Each charge is then at the same distance \(\sqrt{r^{2} + a^{2}}\) from P, so the two fields have EQUAL magnitudes:
\(E_{+q} = E_{-q} = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}\left(r^{2} + a^{2}\right)}\)
Resolve each into components along and perpendicular to the dipole axis. The components PERPENDICULAR to the axis are equal and opposite and CANCEL. The components PARALLEL to the axis both point from \(+q\) towards \(-q\), that is ANTIPARALLEL to \(\vec{p}\), and therefore ADD:
\(\vec{E} = -\left(E_{+q} + E_{-q}\right)\cos\theta\ \hat{p}\)
From the geometry \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{r^{2} + a^{2}}}\), so
\(E = \dfrac{2q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}\left(r^{2} + a^{2}\right)} \times \dfrac{a}{\left(r^{2} + a^{2}\right)^{1/2}} = \dfrac{2qa}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}\left(r^{2} + a^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\)
Writing the dipole moment \(p = q(2a)\):
\(\vec{E} = -\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}\left(r^{2} + a^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\)
The DIRECTION is OPPOSITE to the dipole moment — on the equatorial plane the field points antiparallel to \(\vec{p}\), whereas on the axis it points along \(\vec{p}\).
(I) AT THE CENTRE OF THE DIPOLE, \(r = 0\):
\(\vec{E} = -\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}a^{3}}\)
(II) AT A POINT \(r \gg a\), the \(a^{2}\) is negligible beside \(r^{2}\):
\(\vec{E} = -\dfrac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{3}}\)
The \(\dfrac{1}{r^{3}}\) dependence is the signature of a dipole: its field dies away faster than a point charge's \(\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\), because at large distances the two opposite charges very nearly cancel.
(ii) NET FLUX THROUGH THE CUBE.
The field \(\vec{E} = (10x + 5)\hat{i}\) points along x only, so it is PARALLEL to four of the cube's faces and passes through them without contributing any flux. Only the two faces perpendicular to the x-axis matter.
Take the left face at \(x = 0\) and the right face at \(x = L\), each of area \(L^{2}\).
LEFT FACE. Its outward normal points in \(-\hat{i}\), against the field, so the flux is negative. At \(x = 0\) the field is \(E_{L} = 10(0) + 5 = 5\):
\(\phi_{L} = -E_{L}L^{2} = -5L^{2}\)
RIGHT FACE. Its outward normal points in \(+\hat{i}\), with the field. At \(x = L\) the field is \(E_{R} = 10L + 5\):
\(\phi_{R} = +E_{R}L^{2} = (10L + 5)L^{2}\)
NET FLUX:
\(\phi_{net} = \phi_{L} + \phi_{R} = -5L^{2} + (10L + 5)L^{2}\)
\(\phi_{net} = L^{2}\left(-5 + 10L + 5\right)\)
\(\phi_{net} = 10L^{3}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)
The constant 5 cancels exactly, and that is the physics of the result: a UNIFORM field contributes nothing to the flux through a closed surface, since whatever enters one face leaves the other. Only the part of the field that VARIES with x survives. By Gauss's law this flux implies an enclosed charge \(q = \varepsilon_{0} \times 10L^{3}\).
